neighbours.label: Daoism in English: the Tao (Dao) as the Way, the Tao Te Ching, Laozi, Zhuangzi and wu wei; Confucian, Mohist and Buddhist teaching in the same frames and the ordinary word 'way' stay low
fire: The old gardener said he tried to live by the Tao, letting things grow in their own time.
A new translation of the Tao Te Ching came out this spring.
According to legend, Laozi rode an ox out of China and was never seen again.
Zhuangzi wrote of a cook whose knife never dulled because he followed the Dao.
Wu wei, the Daoist ideal of effortless action, is often misread as laziness.
Daoist sages praised water for overcoming the hard by being soft.
In the Taoist view, naming a thing already separates it from the Way.
The temple's priests trace their lineage back to Laozi.
quiet: The old gardener said he tried to live by the almanac, planting in its own time.
A new translation of the Analects came out this spring.
According to legend, Confucius wandered from state to state looking for a ruler.
Mozi wrote of a builder whose walls never fell because he loved all people equally.
Filial piety, the Confucian ideal of respect for parents, is often misread as obedience.
Buddhist monks praised patience for overcoming anger.
In the Mohist view, every custom must be judged by its usefulness.
The cafe's owners say they found their way back to their hometown.
neighbours.short: Daoism in English (the Tao, Laozi, wu wei)
